title: Quinnipiac hockey opener: big, stunning 10-2 rout of UNH - Total Apex Sports
content: Home > College Sports > Quinnipiac hockey opener: big, stunning 10-2 rout of UNH The Quinnipiac hockey opener was a 10-2 rout of New Hampshire, with four first-period goals and a first win for goalie Christian Kirsch in Hamden. The Quinnipiac hockey opener turned into a rout Friday night, as No. 7 Quinnipiac beat New Hampshire 10-2 before a sellout crowd at M&T Bank Arena in Hamden, Connecticut. The Bobcats scored 10 goals for the first time since 2013, the school said. Quinnipiac scored four times in the first period and led 4-0 after 20 minutes. The Bobcats followed with three goals in the second and three more in the third, according to New Hampshire’s game recap. New Hampshire scored twice in the second period. Freshman Mason Zebeski scored at 13:33, and senior assistant captain Nick Ring scored on the power play at 17:01. Ethan Wyttenbach had two goals and an assist, and Chris Pelosi added two goals. Alex Kostov had two assists in his college debut. Parker Alcos and Dylan Edwards each scored their first collegiate goals, Quinnipiac’s recap said. Goaltender Christian Kirsch earned his first college win with 21 saves on 23 shots. Sixteen Bobcats skaters recorded a point, the most since January 2024. The 10 goals also marked the second-highest total in a season opener in program history, behind a 12-goal game against St. John’s in 1981-82. New Hampshire used two goalies. Michael Simpson made 16 saves, and Teagan Kendrick stopped nine in relief. Quinnipiac hosts Merrimack on Saturday at 4 p.m. EDT at M&T Bank Arena. New Hampshire (0-1) opens Hockey East play at Merrimack on Oct. 8 at 7 p.m., then plays two games at Colgate on Oct. 16-17. title: ROUNDUP: No. 7 Quinnipiac opens with 10-2 drubbing of UNH - USCHO.com
content: Quinnipiac wasted little time showing off its offensive firepower Friday night, scoring four times in the opening 14 minutes and cruising to a 10-2 victory over New Hampshire in the season opener for both teams. Ethan Wyttenbach and Chris Pelosi each scored twice for the Bobcats, who had nine different players record goals and finished with a 35-23 advantage in shots. Wyttenbach opened the scoring just 2:29 into the game before Tyler Borgula, Dylan Edwards and Matthew Lansing added first-period goals to give Quinnipiac a 4-0 lead after 20 minutes. Braden Blace made it 5-0 just 26 seconds into the second before New Hampshire finally broke through on Mason Zebeski’s goal at 13:33. Pelosi answered with a power-play goal less than two minutes later, and after Nick Ring scored on the power play for the Wildcats at 17:01, Wyttenbach responded just 19 seconds later to send Quinnipiac into the third leading 7-2. The Bobcats added three more in the final period, getting a power-play goal from Mason Marcellus just 16 seconds after the opening faceoff before Parker Alcos and Pelosi closed out the scoring 30 seconds apart midway through the period. Christian Kirsch made 21 saves for Quinnipiac, which finished 2-for-5 on the power play and won 45 of 65 faceoffs. No. 10 Massachusetts became the first ranked team to fall this season, dropping a 2-0 road decision to Colorado College on Friday night. Mats Lindgren scored the only goal Colorado College would need at 14:09 of the first period, and goaltender Jackson Unger made the lead stand up with a 32-save shutout. Massachusetts had three power-play opportunities but could not convert. The Minutemen pushed in the third, outshooting Colorado College 15-13 in the period, but Unger turned aside everything he faced. Drew Montgomery sealed the win with an empty-net goal with 13 seconds remaining. Ethan Eskit was sharp in defeat for Massachusetts, stopping 34 of 35 shots as Colorado College finished with a 36-32 edge in shots. Defending national champion Denver opened its title defense with a 6-2 victory over Alaska Anchorage on Friday night. Tye Spencer gave Alaska Anchorage an early lead just 1:41 into the game, but Daxon Rudolph tied it midway through the first before Denver took control with four goals in the second period. Kieran Cebrian scored shorthanded 1:15 into the period, Cale Ashcroft made it 3-1 at 6:12 and, after Spencer answered on the power play, Sam Harris and Jake Fisher scored 14 seconds apart to push the lead to 5-2. Fisher added his second goal of the night midway through the third. Denver finished with a 39-16 advantage in shots and held Alaska Anchorage to just three shots in the final period. Johnny Hicks made 14 saves for the Pioneers, while William Gramme stopped 33 shots for Alaska Anchorage. Michigan broke open a tie game with three second-period goals and rolled to a 7-2 victory over Bowling Green on Friday night in the season opener for both teams. J.P. Hurlbert gave the Wolverines an early lead at 5:01 of the first period, but Jérémie Minville answered on the power play just over two minutes later to send the teams to the first intermission tied 1-1. Michigan then took control in the second, getting goals from Cole McKinney and Michael Hage 2:14 apart before Jayden Perron made it 4-1 at 12:19. Garrett Schifsky extended the lead just 1:31 into the third before Hage scored his second of the night midway through the period. Maxwell Martin added Bowling Green’s second goal at 13:11, but Malcolm Spence closed the scoring for Michigan with 2:23 remaining. Jack Ivankovic made 29 saves for the Wolverines, including 17 in the third period as Bowling Green generated 18 of its 31 shots over the final 20 minutes. Michigan finished with a 42-31 advantage in shots and scored once on five power-play opportunities. Fresh off its national championship game appearance in April, No. 6 Wisconsin built a three-goal lead through two periods and held off Robert Morris for a 4-2 victory Friday night. Luke Osburn opened the scoring for the Badgers at 17:03 of the first period before Bruno Idzan doubled the lead midway through the second. Dylan Compton then made it 3-0 with a power-play goal at 16:13 as Wisconsin outshot Robert Morris 21-6 in the period and 33-9 through 40 minutes. Robert Morris got on the board on Dominic Elliott’s power-play goal 3:14 into the third, but Finn Brink restored Wisconsin’s three-goal lead with a shorthanded goal at 15:26. George Krotiris scored with two seconds remaining to account for the final margin. Alexis Cournoyer made 16 saves in his Wisconsin debut, while Charlie Schenkel stopped 34 shots for Robert Morris. The Badgers finished with a 38-18 advantage in shots. No. 5 Minnesota Duluth survived a strong challenge from LIU, scoring four times in the third period to pull away for a 7-4 victory Friday night. The Bulldogs led 2-0 after first-period goals from Barrett Hall and Adam Kleber, but LIU answered with three goals in the second. Luc Bydal scored twice in a span of 3:37 before Hunter Anderson briefly restored Minnesota Duluth’s lead. Luca Leighton tied the game at 3-3 with 3:10 remaining in the period. LIU then took its first lead just 3:08 into the third on Brennan Nelson’s goal, but Jayson Shaugabay answered only 12 seconds later. Luke Bibby put Minnesota Duluth back in front for good at 13:57, and Callum Arnott followed 50 seconds later with a power-play goal to make it 6-4. Ty Hanson added a shorthanded empty-net goal with 21 seconds remaining. Minnesota Duluth finished with a 36-23 advantage in shots, while Ethan Dahlmeir made 19 saves for the Bulldogs. After a tumultuous month away from the rink, Arizona State opened its season with a convincing 5-0 victory over Lindenwood on Friday night. The Sun Devils are playing without head coach Greg Powers, who was placed on paid administrative leave this week while the university continues to investigate the Aug. 20 workout in which defenseman Matthew Mayich suffered exertional heat stroke and remains in a coma. Assistant coach Mike Corbett is leading the team in Powers’ absence. Ben Muthersbaugh opened the scoring on the power play at 16:47 of the first period before Kyle Smolen made it 2-0 with 33 seconds remaining in the second. Arizona State then broke the game open in the third, getting goals from Olivier Houde, Sean McGurn and Daniel Shlaine. Samuel Urban stopped all 37 shots he faced to earn the shutout as Lindenwood matched Arizona State with 37 shots. The Sun Devils finished 2-for-5 on the power play and killed all five Lindenwood opportunities. Maryville made an immediate statement in its transition to Division I hockey, rallying from two goals down to stun St. Lawrence, 3-2, Friday night at Appleton Arena. St. Lawrence built a 2-0 lead on Cooper Pierson’s power-play goal at 7:09 of the first period and Luke Posthumus’ goal 5:18 into the second. But Maryville began its comeback late in the middle period when Antoine Dorion scored shorthanded at 18:10. Dorion struck again on the power play at 10:03 of the third to tie the game before Gustavs Ozolins completed the comeback with 1:01 remaining in regulation, giving the Saints their first victory over an NCAA Division I opponent during their transition season. St. Lawrence finished with 29 shots and got 25 saves from Cameron Smith. Dorion led Maryville with two goals and an assist. No. 14 Minnesota at No. 19 Michigan Tech (PPD, poor ice conditions) The only opening-night matchup between nationally ranked teams never got underway Friday, as No. 14 Minnesota’s game at No. 19 Michigan Tech was postponed because of unplayable ice conditions at John MacInnes Student Ice Arena. Michigan Tech cited player safety in making the decision. The series will now begin Saturday at 4:07 p.m. ET, with Friday’s postponed game rescheduled for Sunday at 3:07 p.m. ET. Tynan Lawrence scored 1:18 into overtime to lift No. 16 Boston University past Alaska, 2-1, Friday night. Jack Murtagh gave the Terriers the lead at 3:58 of the first period, but Linden Burrett answered on the power play less than three minutes later. Lawrence ended it on BU’s fourth shot of overtime, giving the Terriers the win after assisting on Murtagh’s opening goal. title: USNH Launches New Free Tuition Program For New Hampshire Families Making Up To $100K - Patch
content: A UNH education is now within reach for more New Hampshire families, thanks to the New Hampshire Promise, a new program launched by the University System of New Hampshire. Beginning in fall 2027, incoming first-year and transfer students from families earning up to $100,000 a year can have their tuition covered at any USNH institution, removing a major financial barrier and giving more students the opportunity to pursue their goals and build their future in New Hampshire. “New Hampshire’s public institutions of higher education are a transformative opportunity for students,” USNH Chancellor Cathy Provencher says. “In launching this new program, all of the university system institutions are working together to make higher education more accessible for more New Hampshire students, enabling them to pursue their dreams right here in the Granite State.” Under the terms of the program, New Hampshire residents who are admitted as full-time, first-year students or transfers who have graduated from a New Hampshire community college, with total family income of up to $100,000, qualify to attend a USNH institution — UNH Durham, UNH Manchester, UNH College of Professional Studies Online, Plymouth State University, and Keene State College — tuition-free. With New Hampshire’s median household income of $99,782, according to recent U.S. Census Bureau data, the program has the potential to benefit a significant portion of the state’s families. Admitted students who submit a Free Application for Federal Student Aid (FAFSA) will automatically be considered for the New Hampshire Promise; there is no separate application process. While the program covers tuition, it does not cover housing, food, books, or fees. “The New Hampshire Promise program is an investment in our students and in the future of our state. By expanding affordable pathways to higher education, we’re creating more opportunities for our young people to pursue good-paying jobs and making it easier for them to build their careers in New Hampshire,” says New Hampshire Gov. Kelly Ayotte. “I thank the University System of New Hampshire for their efforts to make college more affordable for New Hampshire students and their families.” The New Hampshire Promise replaces USNH’s Granite Guarantee program, established in 2017 to provide free tuition to Pell-eligible New Hampshire students. Since its inception, more than 4,000 students have qualified for this program. Currently enrolled USNH undergraduates will remain in Granite Guarantee to ensure no disruption of financial aid benefits. The program is the latest effort to make college more affordable in the Granite State. Last month, the University of New Hampshire announced that it awarded a record $40 million in financial aid to incoming students this year, with the average student award topping $16,000. Almost every student in the incoming class (96%) received financial aid, with an average award of $16,918, an increase of more than 50% from the prior year. These efforts, combined with UNH’s high student success rates, led to UNH being named New England’s No. 1 best value public university for the sixth consecutive year, according to the Best Value Schools rankings of National Universities by U.S. News & World Report. According to UNH’s most recent graduating class survey data, UNH graduates boast a 94% success rate, with 71.6% of students employed within 12 months after graduation and another 22.2% enrolled in further education. Additionally, the significant majority of employed graduates — 88% — reported that their job was directly or somewhat related to their major.

The Trump administration is reportedly looking to deploy a Pentagon-built artificial intelligence system to help establish benchmark prices for critical minerals. Officials will initially apply the U.S. Department of War’s Open Price Exploration for National Security (OPEN) AI pricing model to four critical minerals: germanium, gallium, antimony, and tungsten, according to a Reuters report on Tuesday. The OPEN program focuses on metals that are traded in very low volumes. Next year, it will move under the control of the non-profit Critical Minerals Forum (CMF). CMF said it works with government-funded partners to test AI pricing models and support commercially viable mining and processing projects. This comes days after a Bloomberg report stated that the U.S. was moving forward with a price-floor system for critical minerals to reinforce supply chains tied to national security. The plan, crafted by several federal agencies, is being reviewed with allies as Washington looks to shield Western companies from pricing pressure linked to Chinese supply dominance. Trump, who has been very vocal about strengthening the country’s critical minerals supply chain, recently announced that his administration plans to establish a strategic stockpile of critical minerals, supported by $10 billion in initial funding from the U.S. Export-Import Bank. Earlier this month, U.S. Vice President JD Vance introduced a proposal to form a preferred trade bloc among allied nations focused on critical minerals. The plan includes coordinated price floors to reduce China’s influence over materials essential to semiconductors, electric vehicles, and advanced defense systems. China has long dominated the processing of several key minerals and has used that position to influence global supply and pricing. U.S. officials say the new strategy is designed to stabilize markets and help allies diversify supply sources. title: UNH officials say rise in reported rape cases could show more survivors are coming forward - WMUR
content: The new investigation of an alleged rape at Cornell University is drawing attention to college campuses across the country and how they handle assault allegations. The recent Security and Fire Safety Report at the University of New Hampshire shows that reported rape cases are up on and off campus, but the school and advocates argue that could show their efforts to connect victims to resources are working. "As a woman myself, it's terrifying to think about," said UNH sophomore Tess Vallas. Students at UNH said the reports coming out of Cornell University are hard to hear. >> Download the free WMUR app to get updates on the go << "Honestly, it's just really disappointing," said UNH freshman Madeline Dowling. They said it's also hard to hear that their school is reporting a rise in rape cases in the past three years. There were 26 cases reported in 2023, 41 in 2024 and 46 in 2025. "I don't see why that wouldn't be a concern for anyone," Vallas said. "It's not good," said UNH sophomore Tristan White. "It doesn't help either party in the end." UNH said it takes such crimes very seriously and has increased its training to make sure victims have the best support available. School officials said they believe those efforts are why the rape case reports are rising, because more survivors feel comfortable coming forward and not necessarily because more crimes are occurring. UNH offers resources through its SHARPP Center for Interpersonal Violence Awareness, Prevention and Advocacy on campus and partners with the state's Coalition Against Domestic and Sexual Violence to help victims navigate what follows after making a report. "An advocate can help walk a survivor through what each of those are going to look like and what their options are," said Emily Provencher, prevention and child welfare specialist. Those services are available 24/7 and offer a confidential advocate who helps survivors explore their next steps, such as filing a criminal or Title IX complaint or doing nothing at all. Provencher said they're trained to offer the support a survivor needs. "They're going to center everything on what you want and what works best for you," she said. The coalition said that after reports like the Cornell investigation come out, it sees an increase in calls to the center from survivors who feel they can step up after seeing other survivors come forward. If you or someone you know is a victim of sexual abuse, you can call the state's 24/7 sexual assault hotline at 866-644-3574 to be connected with resources. title: UNH Dunkin' Mural: Artist Hides Self-Portrait at MUBkin - Hoodline
content: A massive new mural now stretches across the Dunkin' inside the University of New Hampshire's Memorial Union Building, and if you look closely enough, you might spot the artist herself tucked into the scene wearing a cap and gown. Madeline Pender, a UNH alumna, was hired by Dunkin' to envision and paint the artwork as part of a redesign that turns the beloved campus coffee shop into the chain's first college-campus Signature Series store in New England. Pender painted the mural, which spans the length of the Dunkin' store. She included a self-portrait tucked into the scene. The mural, unveiled Thursday at the Dunkin' location inside the Memorial Union Building, features UNH student athletes, Thomson Hall, the Wildcat statue, and students clutching coffee and donuts, per the same account. It's a fitting tribute for a space students have long called their own. The Memorial Union Building's Dunkin' is so central to daily life on campus that students have nicknamed it “MUBkin,” according to the University of New Hampshire. The store is a familiar campus fixture, and Dunkin' chose it for its signature redesign. Pender also depicted Eli Bryant, a 2024 UNH alumnus and one of her closest friends, standing at an easel inside the mural, according to the Globe's reporting. The artwork he's shown painting on his easel depicts a waterfaring vessel built by UNH students. DriX is an autonomous surface vessel; UNH's Center for Coastal and Ocean Mapping has housed and supported DriX vessels since December 2018, according to UNH's Center for Coastal and Ocean Mapping. The campus landmarks woven throughout the mural carry their own histories. Thomson Hall, one of the primary buildings rendered in the artwork, is a Romanesque structure at the center of campus listed on the National Register of Historic Places, according to Society19. The Wildcat statue is another campus icon featured in the mural. The Memorial Union Building is the setting for the mural. Pender worked with Dunkin' and UNH representatives through several mural iterations before the final design came together, the Globe reports. She hand-painted the design elements herself, and the artwork was then assembled as a digital collage and printed onto the wall covering. The project marks the first Dunkin' Signature Series store on a college campus in New England, per Dunkin'. Pender said senior year was the first time campus life started to feel normal again, the Globe reports, a detail that adds personal weight to her return to UNH as both teacher and muralist. Her mural leaves a lasting imprint at UNH. Pender's mural brings new artwork to the Memorial Union Building. The MUBkin is now home to Dunkin's Signature Series store and Pender's mural. The sprawling mural gives the campus coffee shop a distinctive new look, with a UNH alumna's own face now watching over the counter. title: NH’s public colleges will waive tuition for eligible students - New Hampshire Public Radio
content: Beginning next year, certain students will get free tuition at New Hampshire's state colleges. To be eligible, students must be New Hampshire residents, meet certain academic requirements and be attending one of the schools for the first time. Their families cannot earn more than $100,000 a year. The University System of New Hampshire announced the program, The New Hampshire Promise, Thursday. In a statement, Gov. Kelly Ayotte said tuition waivers will be good for students and employers. “By expanding affordable pathways to higher education, we’re creating more opportunities for our young people to pursue good-paying jobs and making it easier for them to build their careers in New Hampshire,” she said. Under a prior version of the program, which was tied to federal loan eligibility requirements, nearly 4,000 students received tuition waivers between 2017 and this academic year. Tania deLuzuriaga, a University of New Hampshire spokesperson, said they estimate the change in eligibility requirements will mean an additional 29% of next year’s incoming class will qualify for the program. Under the prior program, students had to complete a lengthy and complicated federal Pell Grant application before they knew whether they would qualify for federal aid. That can be a hurdle, deLuzuriaga said, especially for first-generation students whose family members have not navigated the process before. Now, students know up front whether they qualify and only need to fill out the standard federal financial aid application. New Hampshire's public colleges and universities lost nearly $20 million in the last state budget. That prompted UNH to cut $17.5 million from its budget, leading to staff cuts and a hiring freeze. Student enrollment has also been declining. Kimberly DeRego, chief enrollment officer for the University System of New Hampshire, said in an email that the schools will pay for the tuition waivers with money from its endowment. The University System also hopes the new program will attract donors who want to support lower-income students. Students can enroll at UNH, Plymouth State University, Keene State College and UNH’s College of Professional Studies online program, and do not have to live on campus. They must have earned at least a 2.7 GPA at their prior school and be a full-time student. The waivers could save students between $12,000 and $16,000 a year in tuition, depending on where they enroll. Tuition for UNH’s College of Professional Studies costs about $7,700 a year. Students will still have to pay for room and board and fees. The tuition waiver is available only to first-year students and transfer students who have earned an associate's degree at one of the state’s community colleges. It is not open to current students unless they are receiving tuition waivers under the prior program. Students will continue receiving tuition waivers throughout their college degree as long as they continue to meet the eligibility requirements. Students do not have to apply to be considered. The University System will use information from the federal student loan application to determine if they are eligible. Saint Anselm College in Manchester began its own tuition waiver program last year for New Hampshire and Maine students. Last month, it announced it was explaining eligibility to Vermont students. title: USNH launches free tuition program for New Hampshire families making up to $100K - WMUR
content: A college education could soon be more affordable for some Granite State families. Starting next fall, the University System of New Hampshire will cover tuition for eligible in-state students from families making up to $100,000 per year. "We wanted to launch this program called the New Hampshire Promise to cover the cost of tuition for New Hampshire residents who make up to $100,000," said Kim DeRego, UNH vice provost for enrollment management. The New Hampshire Promise program applies to full-time first-year students and qualifying transfers at the University of New Hampshire, Plymouth State University and Keene State College. Some current students said the program sounds like a good idea. "That would be nice," said UNH senior Pacy Morgado. "I mean, I'm in-state, so, obviously, it's the highest in-state tuition in the country, so that would be helpful." "It's pretty exciting news," said UNH sophomore Brynna Kurspahic. "I've had a couple of friends that haven't been able to come back to school because they can't afford it anymore." The program will eventually replace a current one called the Granite Guarantee, and students will remain tuition-free for as long as they're eligible. A New Hampshire resident attending UNH can expect to pay $16,304 per year in tuition. Then, between housing, food and other fees, they have another $19,452 in costs. That adds up to more than $35,000 per year. Students in the program can get additional financial help in other ways. "Families can qualify for lots of other types of aid, including government aid and loans and things like that and other grant programs that are available," DeRego said. Some current students said they're worried about what the program could mean for their tuition, but university officials said there will be no impact. "We are not lowering the scholarships for students in order to fund these," DeRego said. "We're really trying to make the campus experience affordable for all of our students." Students don't need to apply for the program. They will be automatically considered when they fill out their FAFSA. title: UNH, Keene, Plymouth offer free tuition to NH families earning up to $100K - Seacoastonline.com
content: DURHAM — The University System of New Hampshire is rolling out a free tuition program in fall 2027 for all newly enrolled in-state students whose families earn a maximum of $100,000 annually. First-year students and transfer students who previously earned an associate degree through the state’s community college system are eligible for the program to be offered at the University of New Hampshire, Keene State College and Plymouth State University. The new USNH program, New Hampshire Promise, will launch ahead for the 2027-2028 academic year and replace the Granite Guarantee program, which currently offers free tuition to Pell grant-eligible in-state students. “New Hampshire’s public institutions of higher education are a transformative opportunity for students,” USNH Chancellor Cathy Provencher said in a prepared statement Oct. 1. “In launching this new program, all of the university system institutions are working together to make higher education more accessible for more New Hampshire students, enabling them to pursue their dreams right here in the Granite State.” The median household income in New Hampshire is just over $99,000, as last reported by the U.S. Census Bureau. Tania deLuzuriaga, a spokesperson for UNH, said the school projects 29% more incoming UNH students will be eligible for New Hampshire Promise than the existing Granite Guarantee program it is replacing. An average of 900 to 1,000 UNH students enroll via the Granite Guarantee program per year, according to deLuzuriaga. “When President (Elizabeth) Chilton got here a little over two years ago, she wanted to shift our need-based program into something income-based just so it was something more families could take advantage of,” she said. Students enrolling at UNH Manchester and for the university’s online courses will be eligible for the new program, too. The university system will not cap the number of students that can enroll in the New Hampshire Promise program. All admitted students meeting the income and education standards, in addition to a minimum 2.7 grade point average requirement, will be automatically accepted after filing their Free Application for Federal Student Aid (FAFSA). There is no separate application to enroll in New Hampshire Promise when the program takes effect. The free tuition will remain in effect should a future student enroll in another USNH institution, so long as they continue to meet the income and education guidelines. “Awards will be based on an annual review of a student’s FAFSA, academic status, and full-time student status,” USNH says. Created in 2017, the Granite Guarantee program will be phased out in several years. Over 4,000 in-state students within the university system have qualified for the program since its founding. Current Granite Guarantee students cannot join the New Hampshire Promise program, though they will retain their financial assistance for the remainder of their undergraduate studies. In-state tuition at UNH’s flagship Durham campus currently stands at $16,304 per year, excluding room and boarding costs. New Hampshire students pay $15,444 per year at Plymouth State University and $12,348 per year at Keene State College. Before the 2025-2026 school year, in-state tuition rates across the university system were unfrozen for the first time in six years. The tuition aid program announcement comes amid declining undergraduate enrollment at UNH’s Durham and Manchester campuses and in its online student population. Last semester, 11,948 full- and part-time undergraduate students attended UNH, down from 13,631 students in the fall 2016 semester, according to a university dashboard.

title: Families earning up to $100,000 per year will be eligible for free in-state tuition at public N.H. universities - The Boston Globe
content: DURHAM, N.H. — Incoming college students from New Hampshire whose families earn up to $100,000 per year will soon qualify for free tuition at any of the three institutions that comprise the University System of New Hampshire, officials announced Thursday. A new program, called the New Hampshire Promise, will be available to Granite Staters enrolling for the first time in fall 2027 at the University of New Hampshire, Keene State College, and Plymouth State University.
